summary: Defines managed objects for DS1 interfaces, the T1-style digital telephone circuits, for use with network management. It was replaced by RFC 1406.

eli5.summary: It is a checklist for watching a digital phone line used for data.

questions: what are errored seconds in a ds1
subtitle: SNMP managed objects for watching DS1 (T1 and E1) lines: configuration, alarms and error counts in 15-minute buckets.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a standard way to monitor DS1 digital circuits, the T1 and E1 lines terminated by channel service units (CSUs), from an SNMP management station.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB module defines five groups of read-only objects: configuration, interval, current, total and fractional. They follow the error statistics that deployed AT&T ESF CSUs already report, and also apply to D4 and G.704 devices.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1232 was updated by RFC 1239 and then obsoleted by RFC 1406.

facts.value: 320 or more Code Violation events, or one or more Out of Frame events

facts.value: 24 for ESF and D4, 32 for G.704

today: RFC 1232 has been obsoleted by RFC 1406 and was updated by RFC 1239, so the newer RFC 1406 is the one to consult for DS1 managed objects.

sections.title: Place in the Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1232 defines objects for managing DS1 interfaces with the SNMP protocol. It is a product of the Transmission MIB Working Group, and the abstract calls it an experimental portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for TCP/IP-based internets. A companion document covers DS3 objects.

It sits inside the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: RFC 1155 (the SMI, which describes and names objects, with RFC 1212 giving a more concise description mechanism), RFC 1213 (MIB-II, the core objects) and RFC 1157 (SNMP, the protocol used to reach them).

Objects are defined with a subset of ASN.1. Each has a name that is an object identifier, a syntax and an encoding. The module is placed at { experimental 2 }.
sections.eli5: Managing a network device is like reading a dashboard. This document says which dials a digital phone line should have and what to call each one, so every manager can read them the same way.

sections.title: Scope and Objectives
sections.content:
The objects apply when an interface is realized on a DS1 physical interface. That covers two ifType values in the Internet-standard MIB: ds1 (18) and e1 (19). The definitions are based on the AT&T T-1 specifications and Extended Superframe (ESF) format, and the T1 and E1 line disciplines are described as similar enough that separate MIBs are unwarranted.

The aim is the common management of CSUs, both in-chassis and external via proxy. The designers aligned the MIB closely with objects that can be read from deployed ESF CSUs conforming to AT&T specifications, and generalized it to cover D4 and G.704 devices.

One physical DS1 can be multiplexed into several MIB interfaces, or physical interfaces can be concatenated into one logical interface. So each agent assigns a small positive integer, the CSUIndex, to every CSU, which also serves as the key for tabular DS1 data. The mapping between CSU indices and ifIndex values is in the configuration table.
sections.eli5: A phone line can be split into several pretend lines, or several lines can be joined into one. Each box on the line gets its own number so the manager knows which one a reading is about.

sections.title: DS1 Error and Alarm Terms
sections.content:
The RFC defines the events that the counters are built on.

  • An Out of Frame event is declared on two or more framing-bit errors within a 3 millisecond period, or two or more errors out of five or fewer consecutive framing bits.
  • Loss of Signal is declared after 175 +/- 75 contiguous pulse positions with no pulses.
  • A Code Violation Error Event is a received CRC code that does not match the locally calculated one.
  • An Errored Second has one or more Code Violation events or one or more Out of Frame events. A Severely Errored Second has 320 or more Code Violation events or one or more Out of Frame events.
  • The Unavailable Signal State starts at the onset of 10 consecutive Severely Errored Seconds and clears at the onset of 10 consecutive seconds with none.

A Red Alarm is declared because of an incoming Loss of Signal, Loss of Framing or Alarm Indication Signal; the device then sends a Yellow Signal, and the far end declares a Yellow Alarm, in effect making the circuit a one way link. The RFC also admits that successive reads of the severely errored and unavailable second counters can differ if they happen early in a 900 second window, an unavoidable side effect of basing the MIB on deployed AT&T objects.
sections.eli5: The line counts bad seconds. A bad second is one where the signal got scrambled or lost its place. If there are ten very bad seconds in a row, the line is called unavailable until it behaves for ten seconds in a row.

sections.title: The Five Object Groups
sections.content:
The module defines five groups of objects, all read-only in the definitions. The RFC says an agent may make the configuration objects read-write so that an authorized management station can, for example, place the device into a loopback state or start a QRSS bit error rate test.

The configuration group (ds1ConfigTable) is mandatory for every system that attaches to a DS1. Its entries include the CSU index, the interface index, time elapsed in the current period, the number of valid intervals, ds1LineType, ds1ZeroCoding, ds1Loopback, ds1SendCode, the yellow and red alarm flags and a circuit identifier of up to 255 characters set by the circuit vendor.

Line types are ESF, D4, ANSI ESF, G.704 and G.704 with CRC. Zero coding values are jammed bit, B8ZS, inverted HDLC, HDB3 and ZBTSI; with jammed bit, only seven bits per channel, or 1.344 Mbps, remain for data.

The interval, current and total groups carry the same seven counters: Errored Seconds, Severely Errored Seconds, Severely Errored Framing Seconds, Unavailable Seconds, Controlled Slip Seconds, Bipolar Violations and Code Violations. The fractional group maps DS1 channels to interface indices, and is mandatory only for systems using fractional DS1.
sections.eli5: There are five folders. One describes the line, three hold report cards for different time spans, and one says which slices of the line belong to which pretend line.

sections.title: Intervals and Fractional DS1
sections.content:
Statistics are collected in 15 minute intervals. The interval table keeps the previous 96 completed intervals, which covers the past 24 hours. Interval number 1 is the most recently completed one and 96 is the least recent. The current table counts the ongoing 15 minute interval, and the total table holds the cumulative sum for the 24 hour period before the first valid interval. If a CSU came online within the last 24 hours, ds1ValidIntervals shows only the complete intervals it has.

Some deployed CSUs do not record every statistic, so agents may treat unsupported objects as not-accessible. For example, D4 and G.704 (section 2.1.3.2) interfaces do not support Code Violation Error Events.

For fractional DS1, the configuration value ds1Index is 0 and the fractional table lists the channels that support each logical interface. ESF, D4 and ANSI ESF lines have 24 channels numbered 1 through 24. G.704 has 32 channels, where channel 1 is overhead, and G.704 with CRC also uses channel 17 as overhead.
sections.eli5: The line writes a report every fifteen minutes and keeps a whole day of them. If only part of the line is rented, a table says which numbered slices belong to which customer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states simply that security issues are not discussed in the memo. Its only access-related remark is the possibility, noted above, that an agent may expose normally read-only configuration objects as read-write to an appropriately authorized management station, for example to put a CSU into a loopback state.
sections.eli5: The authors did not write anything about keeping bad guys out. They only note that some settings could be made changeable by managers who are allowed to change them.
